events.title: Amazon Dynamo paper published
events.summary: Amazon published the Dynamo paper at SOSP in October 2007 — describing a highly available key-value store that influenced [NoSQL] databases.
events.about: Dynamo's consistent hashing, vector clocks, and quorum reads inspired Cassandra, Riak, and DynamoDB — the blueprint for eventually consistent systems at scale. Every 'AP over CP' debate in distributed systems classes cites this paper.

narrative.whyChosen: The Dynamo paper defined the architectural pattern for hyperscale key-value stores.
narrative.whyImportant: It legitimized eventual consistency for production ecommerce workloads.
narrative.problemSolved: [Relational database]s could not scale horizontally for Amazon's shopping cart during outages.

events.title: Rich Hickey releases Clojure
events.summary: Rich Hickey publicly released Clojure on October 16, 2007 — a Lisp on the [JVM] with immutable data and software transactional memory.
events.about: Clojure brought [functional programming] to [Java] shops without giving up the [JVM] ecosystem. Hickey's 'Simple Made Easy' talks influenced how developers think about state, complexity, and design.

narrative.whyChosen: Clojure proved Lisp could thrive on the [JVM] for production services.
narrative.whyImportant: Immutable data and STM offered a distinct concurrency model from mainstream [OOP].
narrative.problemSolved: [Java] developers wanted functional tools without leaving existing libraries and deployment.

events.title: OAuth 1.0 published
events.summary: The [OAuth] community finalized [OAuth] Core 1.0 on October 24, 2007 — a protocol for delegated [API] access without sharing passwords.
events.about: [OAuth] 1.0 let users grant third-party apps limited access to services like photos or tweets using signed requests instead of handing over credentials. Twitter, Flickr, and early social APIs adopted it. The three-legged dance (request token, authorize, access token) was clunky but proved delegated authorization could work at web scale — setting the stage for [OAuth] 2.0 and [OpenID Connect].

narrative.whyChosen: [OAuth] 1.0 was the first grassroots standard for [API] delegation across competing web platforms.
narrative.whyImportant: It established the consent-and-token model that modern identity federation still builds on.
narrative.problemSolved: Apps needed user data from other services without storing passwords or getting full account control.
